claim: A eukaryotic leading/lagging strand replisome comprising 31 distinct polypeptides has been reconstituted.
source: We have reconstituted a eukaryotic leading/lagging strand replisome comprising 31 distinct polypeptides.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Pol ε is active with CMG on the leading strand.
source: Hence, Pol ε is active with CMG on the leading strand, but it is unable to function on the lagging strand, even when Pol δ is not present.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Pol ε is unable to function on the lagging strand, even when Pol δ is not present.
source: Hence, Pol ε is active with CMG on the leading strand, but it is unable to function on the lagging strand, even when Pol δ is not present.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in the results section.

claim: Pol δ-PCNA is the only enzyme capable of extending Okazaki fragments in the presence of Pols ε and α.
source: Conversely, Pol δ-PCNA is the only enzyme capable of extending Okazaki fragments in the presence of Pols ε and α.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5B.

claim: Pol δ-PCNA is suppressed on the leading strand with CMG.
source: We have shown earlier that Pol δ-PCNA is suppressed on the leading strand with CMG (Georgescu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references a previous publication by the same authors.

claim: CMG, the 11-subunit helicase, is responsible for one or both suppression mechanisms that spatially control polymerase occupancy at the fork.
source: We propose that CMG, the 11-subunit helicase, is responsible for one or both of these suppression mechanisms that spatially control polymerase occupancy at the fork.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Eukaryotes use two different DNA polymerases for the leading and lagging strands, Pols ε and δ, respectively.
source: Cellular studies reveal that eukaryotes use two different DNA polymerases for the leading and lagging strands, Pols ε and δ, respectively (Lee et al., 1989; Weinberg and Kelly, 1989; Tsurimoto et al., 1990; Waga and Stillman, 1998; Benkovic et al., 2001; Pursell et al., 2007; Kunkel and Burgers, 2008; Nick McElhinny et al., 2008; Stillman, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Pol α is a 4-subunit enzyme that contains an RNA primase and DNA polymerase activity.
source: Priming is performed by Pol α, a 4-subunit enzyme that contains an RNA primase and DNA polymerase activity and makes short RNA-DNA hybrid primers of 25–35 nucleotides (Kaguni and Lehman, 1988; Waga and Stillman, 1998; Benkovic et al., 2001; Stillman, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pol α makes short RNA-DNA hybrid primers of 25–35 nucleotides.
source: Priming is performed by Pol α, a 4-subunit enzyme that contains an RNA primase and DNA polymerase activity and makes short RNA-DNA hybrid primers of 25–35 nucleotides (Kaguni and Lehman, 1988; Waga and Stillman, 1998; Benkovic et al., 2001; Stillman, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The 11-subunit CMG complex consists of the Mcm2-7 'motor', a GINS heterotetramer, and one Cdc45 subunit.
source: The 11-subunit CMG complex consisting of the Mcm2-7 'motor', a GINS heterotetramer, and one Cdc45 subunit (Moyer et al., 2006; Ilves et al., 2010; Costa et al., 2011; Costa et al., 2014) provides the helicase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CMG provides the helicase activity.
source: The 11-subunit CMG complex consisting of the Mcm2-7 'motor', a GINS heterotetramer, and one Cdc45 subunit (Moyer et al., 2006; Ilves et al., 2010; Costa et al., 2011; Costa et al., 2014) provides the helicase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In vitro synthesis of the leading strand replisome has been accomplished with the purified CMG complex from budding yeast.
source: While in vitro synthesis of the leading strand replisome has been accomplished with the purified CMG complex from budding yeast (Georgescu et al., 2014), the discontinuous lagging strand is a much more difficult process and the number of proteins required for lagging strand synthesis is currently unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and references a previous publication by the same authors.

claim: RPCs contain CMG along with Mcm10, Ctf4, Pol α, Mrc1, Csm3, Tof1, FACT, and Topo I.
source: Thus, RPCs contain CMG along with Mcm10, Ctf4, Pol α, Mrc1, Csm3, Tof1, FACT, and Topo I.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on previous studies of replisome progression complexes.

claim: A 31 protein system performs both leading and lagging strand synthesis and generates Okazaki fragments of a size similar to those observed in cells.
source: We demonstrate here a 31 protein system, requiring the three replicative Pols α, ε, and δ, which performs both leading and lagging strand synthesis and generates Okazaki fragments of a size similar to those observed in cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Bacteria use simple recruitment processes to attract and hold polymerases to the fork.
source: Bacteria use simple recruitment processes to attract and hold polymerases to the fork. These are typically mediated by polymerase interactions with other proteins at the replication fork, such as the helicase and sliding clamps (Benkovic et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Pol α functions with CMG on both the leading and lagging strands.
source: We also find that Pol α functions with CMG on both the leading and lagging strands.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Pol α lacks a proofreading exonuclease and thus has lower fidelity than Pols ε and δ.
source: However, Pol α lacks a proofreading exonuclease and thus has lower fidelity than Pols ε and δ.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge about DNA polymerases.

claim: Pol α extension activity is suppressed by Pol ε on the lagging strand, even though Pol ε is inactive on the lagging strand.
source: Interestingly, Pol α extension activity is suppressed by Pol ε on the lagging strand, even though Pol ε is inactive on the lagging strand.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Pol δ suppresses Pol α on the leading strand despite its inefficient extension of this strand.
source: Likewise, Pol δ suppresses Pol α on the leading strand despite its inefficient extension of this strand.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Pol α was highly active with CMG and completely extended the leading strand.
source: In contrast to our expectations, Pol α was highly active with CMG and completely extended the leading strand (Figure 1B, lanes 4–6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CMG is absolutely required for Pol α leading strand extension.
source: Dropout reactions demonstrated that CMG is absolutely required and therefore Pol α cannot perform this action alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pol α was fully active on unprimed DNA and the primase within Pol α is capable of priming the leading strand directly.
source: However, Pol α was fully active on unprimed DNA and thus the primase within Pol α is capable of priming the leading strand directly, while the polymerase subunit of Pol α is able to extend it (Figure 1B, lanes 1–3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DNA synthesis by Pol α is distributive.
source: A titration of Pol α into reactions with CMG shows an increasing rate of leading strand elongation as the Pol α concentration is raised, indicating that DNA synthesis by Pol α is distributive (autoradiograph illustrated in Figure 1C left panel and quantified on the right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The leading strand is continuously extended to full-length product by Pol α with CMG.
source: The leading strand is continuously extended to full-length product; consequently, once Pol α has switched to the DNA elongation mode, it does not appear to switch back to the priming mode.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the experimental observations.

claim: At 10–20 nM Pol α, Okazaki fragments were in the range of 200 bp, similar to their length in vivo.
source: At 10–20 nM Pol α, a concentration consistent with intracellular concentrations of Pol α subunits (Ghaemmaghami et al., 2003; Kulak et al., 2014), Okazaki fragments were in the range of 200 bp, similar to their length in vivo (Smith and Whitehouse, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1D, with citations to previous studies.

claim: Okazaki fragment size decreases with increasing Pol α concentration, indicating that priming is stochastic.
source: The fact that the Okazaki fragment size decreases with increasing Pol α concentration indicates that priming is stochastic, occurring with lower frequency as the Pol α concentration is decreased (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Small Okazaki fragments are intrinsic to Pol α action with CMG in the absence of nucleosomes.
source: These results demonstrate that small Okazaki fragments are intrinsic to Pol α action with CMG in the absence of nucleosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the experimental observations.

claim: The lagging strand ssDNA did not serve as a template to generate Okazaki fragments when Pol α and RPA were present without CMG.
source: However, the lagging strand ssDNA did not serve as a template to generate Okazaki fragments when Pol α and RPA were present (Figure 2B, lane 6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Lagging strand synthesis by Pol α with CMG supports robust Okazaki fragment production.
source: In contrast, lagging strand synthesis by Pol α with CMG supports robust Okazaki fragment production by Pol α (lane 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The requirement of CMG for Pol α primase activity suggests that Pol α forms a transient but specific interaction with CMG for priming action.
source: The requirement of CMG for Pol α primase activity suggests that Pol α forms a transient but specific interaction with CMG for priming action, since use of a heterologous enzyme to unwind DNA does not support Pol α priming activity.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Neither Ctf4 nor Mcm10 are required for Pol α priming function with CMG in vitro.
source: Although both Ctf4 and the essential Mcm10 proteins are known to bind Pol α (Gambus et al., 2009; Warren et al., 2009), these results demonstrate that neither Ctf4 nor Mcm10 are required for Pol α priming function with CMG in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by experimental data and mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Pol α also primes the leading strand directly and priming is stimulated by the presence of CMG.
source: Consistent with results of Figure 1B, Pol α also primes the leading strand directly and priming is stimulated by the presence of CMG (compare lanes 3 and 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All the restriction fragments are radioactive and therefore Okazaki fragments are synthesized along the entire length of the DNA.
source: The analysis using CMG and Pol α shows that all the restriction fragments are radioactive and therefore Okazaki fragments are synthesized along the entire length of the DNA (lanes 4–9).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Pol α cannot perform priming and extension in the absence of CMG.
source: The analysis also confirms that Pol α cannot perform priming and extension in the absence of CMG (lanes 1–3) and that ϕ29 Pol cannot perform lagging strand synthesis (lanes 13–15).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Pol ε takes over the leading strand from Pol α after this distributive enzyme dissociates from DNA.
source: Pol ε is the leading strand enzyme and presumably takes over the leading strand from Pol α after this distributive enzyme dissociates from DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a presumption based on the experimental design.

claim: Full-length product is observed in all lanes containing Pol ε with Pol α, indicating that after Pol α primes the DNA, Pol ε takes over and rapidly extends the leading strand.
source: The results show full-length product in all the lanes containing Pol ε with Pol α (autoradiograph in Figure 4A left, compare lanes 1–4 with 5–8; the quantification on the right panel is based on the autoradiograph analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). These observations indicate that after Pol α primes the DNA, Pol ε takes over and rapidly extends the leading strand.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At sufficiently high concentrations, RFC/PCNA competes with Pol α and suppress its extension activity with CMG.
source: At sufficiently high concentrations, RFC/PCNA competes with Pol α and suppress its extension activity with CMG, as previously reported without CMG (Mossi et al., 2000) (Figure 4B and quantification analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4B, with a citation to previous work.

claim: RFC/PCNA inhibits Pol α polymerase extension of primers on the lagging strand.
source: The results show that RFC/PCNA also inhibits Pol α polymerase extension of primers on the lagging strand.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the experimental observations.

claim: When Pol ε was added, it took over the leading strand and extended it full length, but lagging strand Okazaki fragments were inhibited.
source: When Pol ε was added, it took over the leading strand and extended it full length (Figure 4C, lane 3); however, lagging strand Okazaki fragments were inhibited, a result we did not expect (lane 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Pol ε activity is suppressed on the lagging strand.
source: The results of Figure 4C indicate that Pol ε activity is suppressed on the lagging strand.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the experimental observations in Figure 4C.

claim: Pol ε suppresses Pol α, suggesting that Pol ε gains access to lagging strand primed sites but is inactive on them.
source: Moreover, Pol ε suppresses Pol α, suggesting that Pol ε gains access to lagging strand primed sites but is inactive on them.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: As Pol ε is titrated into the reaction, Okazaki fragment synthesis is inhibited, confirming that Pol ε suppresses Pol α polymerase but is unable to extend lagging strand primers.
source: As Pol ε is titrated into the reaction, Okazaki fragment synthesis is inhibited, confirming that Pol ε suppresses Pol α polymerase but is unable to extend lagging strand primers (see quantification in Figure 5A, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A combination of Pol ε and RFC/PCNA inhibits Pol α more than either Pol ε or RFC/PCNA alone.
source: Although Pol ε inhibits Pol α on the lagging strand, a combination of Pol ε and RFC/PCNA inhibits Pol α more than either Pol ε or RFC/PCNA alone (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, lanes 1–2 and 4–7 vs lanes 8–11; quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pol δ-PCNA was slow and distributive on the leading strand in the presence of CMG and at 50 mM potassium glutamate.
source: Our earlier study demonstrated that Pol δ-PCNA was slow and distributive on the leading strand in the presence of CMG and at 50 mM potassium glutamate (Georgescu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and references a previous publication by the same authors.

claim: Pol δ-PCNA is highly processive during synthesis of the 5.4 kb primed RPA-coated ϕX174 ssDNA under the 50 mM potassium glutamate conditions.
source: However, Pol δ-PCNA is highly processive during synthesis of the 5.4 kb primed RPA-coated ϕX174 ssDNA under the 50 mM potassium glutamate conditions used in the 3 kb replisome assays (Langston and O'Donnell, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and references a previous publication by the same authors.

claim: RFC/PCNA competes with Pol α on the leading strand, indicating that PCNA is in fact loaded onto the leading strand.
source: However, we have shown in this report that RFC/PCNA competes with Pol α on the leading strand (Figure 4B, lanes 1–5), indicating that PCNA is in fact loaded onto the leading strand.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Pol δ added to the reaction exacerbates inhibition of Pol α in the presence of RFC/PCNA.
source: We demonstrate in Figure 6A that Pol δ added to the reaction exacerbates inhibition of Pol α in the presence of RFC/PCNA, while both Pol α and Pol ε are active in the presence of CMG and the amount of RFC/PCNA used (see quantifications in Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Pol δ-PCNA does not function with CMG and severely competes and limits the function of Pol α with CMG.
source: Hence, Pol δ-PCNA does not function with CMG and severely competes and limits the function of Pol α with CMG.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the experimental observations.

claim: Pol δ was capable of extending Okazaki fragments in the presence of Pol ε, Pol α, RFC, PCNA, and RPA with CMG.
source: In Figure 5B, Pol δ was titrated into lagging strand reactions, and surprisingly, Pol δ was capable of extending Okazaki fragments under these circumstances.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Pol δ is the only polymerase capable of extending Okazaki fragments in the complete system.
source: In fact, it is the only polymerase that we observed to perform this function.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the experimental observations.

claim: CMG does not prevent Pol δ function on the lagging strand, even while Pol δ-PCNA activity is suppressed on the leading strand.
source: Hence, CMG does not prevent Pol δ function on the lagging strand, even while Pol δ-PCNA activity is suppressed on the leading strand.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the experimental observations.

claim: Leading and lagging strand rates are similar using either primed or unprimed DNA forked substrate.
source: While leading and lagging strand rates are similar using either DNA forked substrate, there is 20–25% more synthesis using primed DNA forks relative to unprimed DNA forks.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: This is the first reconstitution of a eukaryotic tri-polymerase leading/lagging strand replisome from purified proteins.
source: The current report is the first reconstitution of a eukaryotic tri-polymerase leading/lagging strand replisome from purified proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a summary of the study's achievement.

claim: Leading/lagging strand replication is recapitulated in vitro with CMG, Pol ε, Pol α, Pol δ, RFC, PCNA, and RPA, comprising 31 different proteins.
source: This report demonstrates that leading/lagging strand replication is recapitulated in vitro with CMG, Pol ε, Pol α, Pol δ, RFC, PCNA, and RPA, comprising 31 different proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Nucleosomes are not needed to size Okazaki fragments in vitro.
source: Hence, nucleosomes are not needed to size Okazaki fragments in vitro, the essential Mcm10 protein that binds Pol α is not required, nor is the Ctf4 trimer that connects Pol α to CMG (Simon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section based on the experimental observations.

claim: The essential Mcm10 protein that binds Pol α is not required for in vitro replication.
source: Hence, nucleosomes are not needed to size Okazaki fragments in vitro, the essential Mcm10 protein that binds Pol α is not required, nor is the Ctf4 trimer that connects Pol α to CMG (Simon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section based on the experimental observations.

claim: The Ctf4 trimer that connects Pol α to CMG is not required for in vitro replication.
source: Hence, nucleosomes are not needed to size Okazaki fragments in vitro, the essential Mcm10 protein that binds Pol α is not required, nor is the Ctf4 trimer that connects Pol α to CMG (Simon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section based on the experimental observations, with a citation to previous work.

claim: Suppression reactions specify correct polymerase placement at the fork and when a polymerase occupies the 'wrong strand' it is excluded from functioning.
source: The current report reveals that suppression reactions specify correct polymerase placement at the fork and that when a polymerase occupies the 'wrong strand' it is excluded from functioning.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a key finding of the study.

claim: Polymerase recruitment by binding clamps and the helicase underlies attraction of polymerases to replication forks of bacteria, its phages, and the SV40 virus.
source: Indeed, polymerase recruitment by binding clamps and the helicase underlies attraction of polymerases to replication forks of bacteria, its phages, and the SV40 virus.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as established knowledge about bacterial and viral replication systems.

claim: Pol ε binds directly to CMG helicase, stabilizing it on the leading strand.
source: For example, Pol ε binds directly to CMG helicase, stabilizing it on the leading strand (Langston et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and references a previous publication by the same authors.

claim: Pol α polymerase activity is highly functional with CMG on both leading and lagging strands in the absence of other polymerases.
source: We were surprised to find that Pol α polymerase activity is highly functional with CMG on both leading and lagging strands in the absence of other polymerases.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section based on the experimental observations.

claim: Pol α does not provide bulk leading or lagging strand synthesis in cells.
source: Pol α lacks the high fidelity of Pols ε and δ and does not provide bulk leading or lagging strand synthesis in cells, and thus processes must exist that suppress the polymerase activity of Pol α.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as established knowledge about cellular replication.

claim: Pol ε is suppressed from function on the lagging strand by the relative orientation in which CMG holds Pol ε.
source: Interestingly, Pol ε is also suppressed on the lagging strand; perhaps, Pol ε is suppressed from function on the lagging strand by the relative orientation in which CMG holds Pol ε.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a speculative explanation for the observed suppression.

claim: The three-polymerase-CMG replisome is the product of polymerase suppression reactions that enable a unique asymmetric arrangement of DNA polymerases to advance the replication fork.
source: Hence, the three-polymerase-CMG replisome is the product of polymerase suppression reactions that enable a unique asymmetric arrangement of DNA polymerases to advance the replication fork.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Pol δ is highly processive with PCNA on primed ssDNA under the conditions of this report.
source: Yeast Pol δ is highly processive with PCNA on primed ssDNA under the conditions of this report (Langston and O'Donnell, 2008), yet Pol δ-PCNA is not effective in extending the leading strand with CMG helicase.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and references a previous publication by the same authors.

claim: The distributive behavior of Pol δ-PCNA with CMG suggests that CMG exerts a negative effect upon Pol δ, causing it to frequently dissociate from PCNA/DNA.
source: The distributive behavior of Pol δ-PCNA with CMG suggests that CMG exerts a negative effect upon Pol δ, causing it to frequently dissociate from PCNA/DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Pol δ self-ejects from PCNA upon completing replication of a template.
source: A possible explanation for how CMG may cause distributive behavior of Pol δ with PCNA/DNA lies in our earlier finding that Pol δ self-ejects from PCNA upon completing replication of a template (Langston and O'Donnell, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and references a previous publication by the same authors.

claim: CMG may occlude the leading strand ssDNA, tricking Pol δ-PCNA to eject as if it were at the end of an Okazaki fragment.
source: A straightforward mechanism could be that CMG occludes the leading strand ssDNA, tricking Pol δ-PCNA to eject as if it were at the end of an Okazaki fragment.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a speculative mechanism.

claim: The Pol2 gene encoding the catalytic polymerase contains two polymerase structures: the active polymerase/exonuclease on the N-terminal half and B-family polymerase in the C-terminal half of Pol2 that is presumed to be inactive.
source: In this connection, the Pol2 gene encoding the catalytic polymerase actually contains two polymerase structures: the active polymerase/exonuclease on the N-terminal half and B-family polymerase in the C-terminal half of Pol2 that is presumed to be inactive (Tahirov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and references a previous publication.

claim: The C-terminal 'inactive polymerase' region of Pol ε is required for cell viability, while the N-terminal region containing the active polymerase is dispensable.
source: Interestingly, genetic studies have shown that the C-terminal 'inactive polymerase' region of Pol ε is required for cell viability, while the N-terminal region containing the active polymerase is dispensable (Dua et al., 1999; Kesti et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and references previous publications.

claim: The binding of Pol ε to CMG involves Dpb2, and possibly the Dpb3, Dpb4 subunits of Pol ε, and regions of Pol2 as well.
source: The binding of Pol ε to CMG involves Dpb2, and possibly the Dpb3, Dpb4 subunits of Pol ε, and regions of Pol2 as well.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section based on previous knowledge.

claim: Expression and purification of a mutant Pol ε that lacks the active N-terminal half of Pol2 (ΔN-Pol ε) yields a 4-subunit complex, while the active polymerase half of Pol ε is monomeric.
source: Expression and purification of a mutant Pol ε that lacks the active N-terminal half of Pol2 (ΔN-Pol ε) yields a 4-subunit complex, while the active polymerase half of Pol ε is monomeric (Hogg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and references a previous publication.

claim: Pol α functions on the leading strand with CMG while Pol δ-PCNA is suppressed, leaving open the possibility that Pol α could participate as the leading strand polymerase in ΔN-Pol ε mutants.
source: However, the finding in this report that Pol α functions on the leading strand with CMG while Pol δ-PCNA is suppressed leaves open the possibility that Pol α could participate as the leading strand polymerase in ΔN-Pol ε mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a speculative possibility based on the experimental findings.

claim: Ctf4/AND-1 is essential in most cells (not in budding yeast).
source: For example, Ctf4/AND-1 is essential in most cells (not in budding yeast), and yeast Ctf4 helps recruit Pol α bind to RPCs (Gambus et al., 2009), yet the current study shows that Pol α functionally interacts with CMG without Ctf4.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and references a previous publication.

claim: Yeast Ctf4 helps recruit Pol α bind to RPCs.
source: For example, Ctf4/AND-1 is essential in most cells (not in budding yeast), and yeast Ctf4 helps recruit Pol α bind to RPCs (Gambus et al., 2009), yet the current study shows that Pol α functionally interacts with CMG without Ctf4.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and references a previous publication.

claim: Pol α functionally interacts with CMG without Ctf4.
source: For example, Ctf4/AND-1 is essential in most cells (not in budding yeast), and yeast Ctf4 helps recruit Pol α bind to RPCs (Gambus et al., 2009), yet the current study shows that Pol α functionally interacts with CMG without Ctf4.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: The essential Mcm10 protein is known to bind Pol α, but Mcm10 is not required for fork function in vitro.
source: Likewise, the essential Mcm10 protein is known to bind Pol α (Warren et al., 2009), but this study shows that Mcm10 is not required for fork function in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section based on the experimental findings, with a citation to previous work.

claim: In vitro fork progression is 4–5 ntds/s, 5–10 times slower than in vivo measurements.
source: It is important to note, however, that in vitro fork progression is 4–5 ntds/s, 5–10 times slower than in vivo measurements, and thus one or more of these proteins may be required to increase the rate of fork movement.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section based on the experimental observations.

claim: Pol α can prime the leading strand directly.
source: The current report also reveals that Pol α can prime the leading strand directly.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: All proposed models of leading strand initiation in bacteria and SV40 show priming on the lagging strand of a bidirectional origin, which becomes the leading strand of one fork, rather than directly priming the leading strands.
source: To our knowledge, before this report, all proposed models of leading strand initiation in bacteria and SV40 show priming on the lagging strand of a bidirectional origin, which becomes the leading strand of one fork, rather than directly priming the leading strands (Waga and Stillman, 1998; Méndez and Stillman, 2003; Kaguni, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and references previous publications.

claim: Pol α is robust in initiating the leading strand directly and targets CMG to do so.
source: Pol α is robust in initiating the leading strand directly and targets CMG to do so.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cellular studies indicate that nucleosomes are involved in determining Okazaki fragment size.
source: Cellular studies indicate that nucleosomes are involved in determining Okazaki fragment size (Smith and Whitehouse, 2012), but data in this report show that short Okazaki fragments of the size observed in vivo do not require nucleosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and references a previous publication.

claim: Short Okazaki fragments of the size observed in vivo do not require nucleosomes.
source: Cellular studies indicate that nucleosomes are involved in determining Okazaki fragment size (Smith and Whitehouse, 2012), but data in this report show that short Okazaki fragments of the size observed in vivo do not require nucleosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: Nucleosomes may still be needed for greater precision in Okazaki fragment length.
source: However, nucleosomes may still be needed for greater precision in Okazaki fragment length.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a speculative possibility.

claim: Pol ε forms a stable and isolable complex with CMG.
source: We also demonstrate that Pol ε forms a stable and isolable complex with CMG, which stands in contrast to the inability to isolate Pol ε in RPCs as defined by a complex that stays associated during two successive affinity columns (Gambus et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section based on the experimental findings, with a citation to previous work.

claim: Some Pol ε can be recovered when isolated in a single-step pull down with epitope tagged CMG from cell extracts.
source: However, some Pol ε can be recovered when isolated in a single-step pull down with epitope tagged CMG from cell extracts (Sengupta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and references a previous publication.

claim: The maximal rate (Vmax) of leading strand replication with Pol α and CMG is 4.5 ± 0.4 ntd/s.
source: The inset graph plots the average replication rate vs the concentration of Pol α; the maximal rate (Vmax) of 4.5 ± 0.4 ntd/s was obtained by fitting of the data with a Michaelis–Menten-type equation.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C and is based on quantitative analysis of the experimental data.

claim: At 10-20 nM Pol α, the average Okazaki fragment size is approximately 70-88 bp.
